title: Newton’s laws of motion
subtitle: Forces, inertia and contact interactions
description: Nine tabs, six interactive experiments, a mean-force calculator, four worked problems and 14 questions: Newton’s laws, friction and elasticity.
alt: A cart accelerated by a force, with force and acceleration vectors pointing in the same direction

intro.title: From describing motion to explaining it
intro.html:
Kinematics describes trajectories, velocity and acceleration. Dynamics connects changes in motion to interactions between bodies. A force can change the velocity vector or deform a body.

What is a principle?

A fundamental law supported by observations and experiments, used as a starting point for a theory. Newton’s laws were published in 1687 and describe macroscopic bodies very well at speeds much lower than the speed of light. They have a limited domain of applicability.

Before you begin

Review mass, vectors, vector addition and resolution, velocity and acceleration. For each situation: choose the body, draw only the forces acting on it, choose axes and apply Newton’s second law.

Lesson route

Explore the three laws, force addition and inertial frames, then friction and elasticity. Change parameters in the experiments; use the problems and quiz to check your interpretation.

Σ F⃗ = m a⃗
p⃗ = m v⃗

The models use g = 9.8 m/s2. Drawings are schematic; numerical values use SI units. Colours distinguish quantities and are accompanied by labels.

inertia.title: First law · Inertia
inertia.html:
In an inertial frame, a particle remains at rest or moves in a straight line at constant velocity if the resultant force acting on it is zero.
Σ F⃗ = 0   ⇒   a⃗ = 0   ⇒   v⃗ = constant

Inertia is the property of bodies to maintain their velocity when the resultant force is zero. Mass measures inertia: the same force produces a smaller acceleration in a more massive body. Inertia is not a force.

Translational equilibrium includes rest and straight-line motion at constant velocity. For extended bodies, complete equilibrium also requires rotational equilibrium. Uniform circular motion is not translational equilibrium: the direction of velocity changes.
inertia.after:
Observe and explain

The rim exerts a force towards the centre. When the rim disappears, the ball leaves along the tangent at the release point, with its velocity at that instant. Resistance is neglected; weight and the vertical normal force balance. A javelin thrown on Earth changes velocity because of gravity and air resistance.

newton2.title: Second law · Force and acceleration
newton2.html:
In an inertial frame, for a constant-mass body, acceleration is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to mass. It points in the direction of the resultant, which need not be the direction of velocity.

Σ F⃗ = m a⃗   ;   a⃗ = Σ F⃗ / m   ;   1 N = 1 kg·m/s2

Experiment on a frictionless horizontal track. Weight and the normal force balance. The horizontal force is the resultant; when F = 0, a moving body maintains its velocity.
newton2.after:
Momentum and mean force

Momentum is the vector p⃗ = m v⃗. For a constant-mass particle, Σ F⃗ = dp⃗/dt. Over a finite interval, Δp⃗/Δt is the mean resultant force; it is not generally the instantaneous force.

F⃗avg = Δp⃗ / Δt = m Δv⃗ / Δt

action.title: Third law · Action and reaction
action.html:
If A exerts a force on B, B simultaneously exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on A. The forces in a pair belong to the same interaction and act on different bodies.

F⃗A→B = −F⃗B→A

They do not cancel in the force balance of a single body. They are internal forces and cancel in the balance for the combined A+B system. Accelerations can differ in magnitude: |a1| / |a2| = m2/m1.
action.after:
Identify the correct pair

A body’s weight and the support’s normal force are not an action–reaction pair: both act on the body. The partner of weight is the body’s gravitational pull on Earth. The partner of the normal force is the body’s push on the support.

Interactions act through contact or fields: a hand pushes an object, and Earth attracts a body. In the particle approximation or for spherically symmetric bodies, gravitational attraction is represented along the line joining the centres.

forces.title: Force superposition and inertial frames
forces.html:
Each interaction contributes to the resultant. Forces and their acceleration contributions add as vectors; their magnitudes cannot simply be added in every situation.

R⃗ = F⃗1 + F⃗2   ;   a⃗ = R⃗ / m
R = √(F12 + F22 + 2F1F2 cos α)
forces.after:
Galilean transformations

Two inertial frames with parallel axes move relative to each other with constant velocity u⃗. If their origins coincide at t = 0 and there is no rotation:

r⃗ = r⃗′ + u⃗t   ;   t = t′
v⃗ = v⃗′ + u⃗   ;   a⃗ = a⃗′

Classical relativity: the laws of mechanics have the same form in all inertial frames. In an accelerating vehicle or a rotating frame, the simple equation Σ F⃗ = m a⃗ for real forces requires frame corrections.

friction.title: Contact interactions · Normal force and friction
friction.html:
A contact force has a normal component N, perpendicular to the surface, and a tangential component: friction. Friction opposes relative sliding or its tendency, not necessarily the body’s velocity relative to the ground.

Static friction

It adjusts to the applied load up to fs,max = μsN. It can be zero; it is not always at its maximum.

0 ≤ fs ≤ μsN

Kinetic friction

In the Coulomb dry-friction model, fk ≈ μkN. It depends on the materials and normal force and is approximately independent of apparent contact area and speed over a limited range. The coefficients are dimensionless; usually μk ≤ μs.

On an incline with no other forces: N = mg cos α and the downhill component of weight is mg sin α. Sliding from rest begins when tan α > μs. The limiting angle satisfies tan φ = μs.
friction.after:
The experiment restarts from rest after each change. During sliding: a = g(sin α − μk cos α). Friction points uphill; at α = 0 and rest, it is zero.

Applications

Friction enables walking, braking, writing and belt drives. Lubricants, bearings and air cushions reduce resistance.

Measure and compare

Use a force meter to pull a body horizontally at constant speed: the reading equals kinetic friction. Calculate μₖ = F/(mg), then repeat with other masses and faces of the same body. Compare with μₛ = tan φ measured at the onset of sliding on an adjustable incline.

hooke.title: Elasticity · Hooke’s law and mechanical stress
hooke.html:
An elastic body returns to its original shape after unloading, within its elastic range. In the linear range, a spring’s restoring force opposes deformation x measured from its natural length.

Fe,x = −kx   ;   |Fe| = k|x|   ;   [k] = N/m

Spring extension: x = Δl = l − l0, where l is the deformed length and l0 the natural length. Under tension x > 0; under compression x < 0.

x = Δl = l − l0
Δl = Fd/k   ;   Δleq = mg/k

Fd is the magnitude of the tensile force balancing the spring force. The formula Δl = Fd/k applies at equilibrium within the proportional range. For a suspended body at rest, Fd = mg. In the animation, x is the instantaneous extension from the natural length; displacement from equilibrium is x − Δleq, while mg/k is only the equilibrium extension.

The force a body applies to a spring and the force the spring applies to the body form an action–reaction pair. On a suspended body in equilibrium, weight and the elastic force balance, but they are not such a pair.
hooke.after:
Mechanical stress and Young’s modulus

For a straight, homogeneous wire of constant cross-sectional area S and initial length l0, under axial loading in the linear range:

σ = Fd/S   ;   ε = Δl/l0   ;   σ = Eε
Δl = Fdl0/(ES)
Fd = (ES/l0) Δl   ;   kwire = ES/l0

σ is stress (Pa), ε is relative strain (dimensionless), and E is Young’s modulus (Pa). The relation k = ES/l0 applies to an axially stretched wire; it is not the general formula for a helical spring.

Indicative values of E: steel ≈ 200 GPa, aluminium ≈ 70 GPa, wood parallel to the grain ≈ 8–15 GPa. Rubber responds strongly to material composition and deformation; a linear model is valid only over a suitable range.

Material stress–strain curves

These schematic curves have no numerical scale and do not represent measurements of a particular material. The vertical axis shows engineering stress σ = Fd/S0; the horizontal axis shows engineering strain ε = Δl/l0. S0 is the initial cross-sectional area. Curve shape depends on the material and test conditions.

Ductile metal · tensile curve
  • O–P: linear range. σ = Eε; the slope is Young’s modulus E. P is the proportionality limit.
  • P–L: nonlinear elastic range. Unloading restores the initial shape, but the linear form of Hooke’s law no longer applies. L is the elastic limit.
  • Beyond L: plastic deformation. Permanent strain remains after unloading; yielding and then strain hardening may occur.
  • M: maximum engineering stress. Necking follows; engineering stress can decrease because it is calculated using the initial area S0.
  • R: fracture. The shape and extent of the regions vary between metals; a distinct yield plateau is not universal.
Brittle material · fracture with little plastic deformation

A brittle material (for example, glass) can fracture at a small strain, with very little plastic deformation. R marks fracture; a yield plateau is not assumed.

Elastomer · nonlinear elasticity

An elastomer can undergo large elastic strains with a nonlinear response. The slope varies, so a single E or k does not describe the entire curve. Loading and unloading are idealized without hysteresis; R marks a schematic fracture limit, without a numerical value.

Determine the spring constant

Fix k. Choose at least five masses and record F = mg and the equilibrium extension Δl. Calculate k = F/Δl for each pair and their mean. The F versus Δl graph has slope k; the Δl versus F graph has slope 1/k. For real measurements, repeat readings and estimate uncertainty. Stay within the spring’s elastic range.

problems: A body with m<sub>1</sub> = 2 kg has a<sub>1</sub> = 8 m/s<sup>2</sup>. What acceleration does a 5 kg body have under the same resultant?
F = m1a1 = 16 N; a2 = F/m2 = 3.2 m/s2.
A 0.2 kg ball starts from rest and reaches 8 m/s in 0.1 s. Calculate the mean resultant in the direction of motion.
Δp = mΔv = 1.6 kg·m/s; Favg = Δp/Δt = 16 N.
A 5 kg body is released on an incline with α = 30°, μ<sub>s</sub> = 0.4 and μ<sub>k</sub> = 0.3. Does it slide? What is its acceleration?
N = mg cos 30° ≈ 42.44 N; mg sin 30° = 24.5 N; fs,max ≈ 16.97 N. It slides because 24.5 > 16.97. fk ≈ 12.73 N; a = (24.5 − 12.73)/5 ≈ 2.35 m/s2 downhill.
A vertical spring with k = 50 N/m supports a 1 kg mass. Find its extension and elastic force at equilibrium.
kΔl = mg ⇒ Δl = 9.8/50 = 0.196 m. The elastic force has magnitude 9.8 N and points upwards.
questions: If the resultant force is zero in an inertial frame, a body…
a⃗ = 0: the body remains at rest or moves in a straight line at constant velocity.
Mass is a scalar quantity and measures inertia.
A 2 kg body has a = 8 m/s². Under the same force, a 5 kg body has…
Which expression in SI base units equals 1 N?
A 0.2 kg ball goes from rest to 8 m/s in 0.1 s. The mean resultant is…
The forces in an action–reaction pair…
are opposite and act on different bodies
They appear simultaneously, have equal magnitudes and act on different bodies.
Two people of 40 kg and 80 kg push each other. Who has the greater acceleration during contact?
The forces have equal magnitudes. Half the mass gives twice the acceleration magnitude.
In the dry-friction model, kinetic friction has magnitude…
fₖ ≈ μₖN. The coefficient is dimensionless.
The angle at which sliding starts from rest satisfies…
At the limit, mg sin φ = μₛ mg cos φ.
At α = 30°, μₛ = 0.4, a 5 kg body released from rest…
slides: 24.5 N exceeds the limit of about 16.97 N
The downhill weight component exceeds maximum static friction.
The elastic-force component along the deformation axis is…
The minus sign shows that the restoring force opposes deformation.
A spring with k = 50 N/m supports 1 kg. Its equilibrium extension is…
A straight wire has k = ES/l₀. If its initial length doubles while E and S remain constant, k…
Axial stiffness is inversely proportional to initial length.
In two inertial frames related by Galilean transformations, acceleration…
The relative velocity of the frames is constant, so a⃗ = a⃗′.
